subject: How to use the 'manual_dispersal_multipliers' or to define odds for states/ranges to go through

messages.author: 5c74d487a8b44dd1
messages.subject: How to use the 'manual_dispersal_multipliers' or to define odds for states/ranges to go through
parts:
If I have 5 states/ranges, and I want to limit the chance of the BioGeoBEARS analysis going through non-adjacent areas. How would I then implement this in a BioGeoBEARS analysis? I think my question relates to this section
http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts
And I might have overlooked the answer.

With 5 state/ranges e.g. A, B, C, D and E.
I would like the BioGeoBEARS analysis to take into consideration that since A and B are next to each other I would like the chance of A and B being more likely in the analysis, than A and C, and since A and D are even further apart (with B and C in between), I would like the chance of this state/range being even smaller.

I have already used these two helpful sections:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#manual_modify_states
http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts#reuse_modified_states
And removed the non-adjacent areas, but I would like to try and reduce dispersal between ranges far apart even further -  i.e. perhaps by making a matrix like this:

    A    B    C    D    E
A    0.00    1.00    0.50    0.33    0.25
B    1.00    0.00    1.00    0.50    0.33
C    0.50    1.00    0.00    1.00    0.50
D    0.33    0.50    1.00    0.00    1.00
E    0.25    0.33    0.50    1.00    0.00

To reflect that the odds for dispersal from A and all the way to E is very hard. Is this would have to go through B, C and D, in this order.
I bit like ordered polarity in cladistic characters.
My first question is: (1) is this possible in BioGeoBEARS, and have I overlooked the answer here: http://phylo.wikidot.com/example-biogeobears-scripts ?
My second question is (2) if I can feed BioGeoBEARS such a matrix, how would it need to make it look like? And is it through this commented line, that I can feed the analysis this information:
#BioGeoBEARS_run_object$dispersal_multipliers_fn = "manual_dispersal_multipliers.txt"

Thanks in advance for any help.

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] How to use the 'manual_dispersal_multipliers' or to define odds for states/ranges to go through
parts:
Hi -- yes, it is possible. The simplest / most natural way to do it is with a distance matrix rather than manual dispersal multipliers.

You define a matrix of relative distances, where 

relative distance = (Great Circle Distance) / (minimum nonzero distance*** between all areas)

Then, you set "x" to be a free parameter, and estimate it along with all of the other parameters during the ML search.  The x parameter modified the base dispersal rates/weights like this:

d_actual = d_base * (relative_distance)^x
j_actual = j_base * (relative_distance)^x

If x is fixed to 0, then the distance has no impact on dispersal probability. This is the null model, and this is what you are already assuming in a standard BioGeoBEARS model with no special multipliers on dispersal probabilities.

If x is free, and inferred to be negative (which is usually the case), then dispersal probability drops off with distance. If x=-1, then doubling the distance halves the dispersal probability.  If x=-2, then dispersal probability drops off with the square of distance.

This method gets you away from the old problem of "how do I objectively decide the manual dispersal multipliers, e.g. should South-America to Africa get a multiplier of 0.1 or 0.001 or what??".  By estimating x, you are estimating the effect of distance on dispersal probability.

This model variant is written up in: Van Dam and Matzke (2016), Journal of Biogeography.

Cheers,
Nick

*** If your minimum distance between 2 areas is 0 because the two areas are touching, you need to think of a slightly more complex solution. E.g., perhaps you use the distances between the center points of regions. Or, perhaps you set the areas-touching distance to 1, and also set the closest nonzero distance to 1, but then use a second matrix (the manual dispersal multiplier matrix) to put a penalty of 0.1 on dispersal when areas are not touching, and then turn on the w parameter and estimate w as a free parameter, so that the parameter for non-touching areas is 0.1^w.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: Re: How to use the 'manual_dispersal_multipliers' or to define odds for states/ranges to go through
parts:
Thanks for a detailed answer. I was not sure as to how the inputfile for a distance matrix should look like, in order to get BioGeoBEARS to accept the input. But having had a look in the supporting information in the paper you recommended (Van Dam and Matzke (2016), Journal of Biogeography)

I came up with this matrix:

 

_____________

A         C         E          I           O         S

0          31800  38100  23100  16500  29700

31800  0          6300    8700    15300  7200

38100  6300    0          15000  21600  10650

23100  8700    15000  0          6600    6600

16500  15300  21600  6600    0          13200

29700  7200    10650  6600    13200  0

 

END

_____________

 

This is based on the map attached showing oceanic regions. If I have understood the instructions correct you advice measuring distances between centers of ranges.

 

It took me some time to work out how a file with a distance matrix should look like, as the BioGeoBEARS support page was missing an example of such a matrix.

But as R and BioGeoBEARS accepted the matrix here above, I assumed it has read the matrix as I intended it to be read.

 

I also tried excluding non-existing joined ranges. Among the 6 ranges ’A, C, E, I, O and S’ in my analysis I excluded the non-adjacent combinations. But this did not appear to return a better LnL value for the traced ranges. Providing the actual distances between the center of each of the ranges returned a better LnL value. But from what I can read on the google group here, and from your paper (2016) in Journal of Biogeography this is to be expected, that multiple restrictions to the analysis does not necessarily add up to a better LnL value. Please let me know if I have misunderstood this part.

 

I am attaching my code and input files and resulting output files (in a tar.gz file). I am also attaching a worldmap showing the 6 ranges ’A, C, E, I, O and S’ in my analysis.

 

As my analysis in BioGeoBEARS behaved alright, and accepted my inputfile I assume I have performed the analysis correct, as I have followed all the instructions on the BioGeoBEARS webpage, but I would appreciate if anyone can spot something I might have overlooked.


I have one additional question. Would it make sense to also feed BioGeoBEARS a 'manual dispersal multiplier matrix' in addition to the one I already have used with the actual distances? That is, would it make sense to feed BioGeoBEARS a matrix with probabilities for dispersal between ranges as well as also feeding it the actual distances? Or will a 'manual dispersal multiplier matrix' just be a reflection of the actual distances once again, and fortify that the ranges are far apart in the BioGeoBEARS analysis?

 

Thanks
